cieloCurConAnd: The princess chained to a rock for her mother Cassiopeia’s vanity and rescued by Perseus. On her hip lies the Andromeda Galaxy, some 2.5 million light years away: the farthest thing visible to the naked eye. Her star Alpheratz was originally shared with Pegasus; the name comes from the Arabic for “the horse”.
cieloCurConAnt: Lacaille’s air pump: the single-cylinder machine the French physicist Denis Papin used for his experiments. He called it la Machine Pneumatique; Francis Baily shortened it to Antlia in 1845. Its brightest star is only fourth magnitude and, as Ridpath puts it, it “contains no objects of note”.
cieloCurConAps: The bird of paradise of New Guinea. Europeans knew it only from skins whose feet and wings the locals had removed; the first were brought back in 1522 by the survivors of Magellan’s voyage round the world, hence the Greek name apous, “footless”. Plancius’s globe labelled it Apis Indica, “Indian bee”: probably a misprint for avis, “bird”.
cieloCurConAqr: The water-bearer: to the Greeks, Ganymede, the young Trojan shepherd whom Zeus, in the form of an eagle, carried off to be cup-bearer of the gods. His jar is a Y of four stars around Zeta Aquarii, and the stream of water runs down to Fomalhaut, which now belongs exclusively to neighbouring Piscis Austrinus.
cieloCurConAql: The eagle of Zeus, which carried his thunderbolts and, in one version of the myth, snatched up Ganymede. The name of its star Altair comes from the Arabic for “the flying eagle”. Its southern part was for Ptolemy another constellation, Antinous, which some maps drew as a young man held in the eagle’s claws; it is now gone: its stars belong to the Eagle today.
cieloCurConAra: The altar on which the gods swore allegiance before fighting the Titans; once they had won, Zeus set it in the sky. It is usually drawn with its base to the north and its flames rising southwards. Ptolemy counted seven stars in it; of the eight Bayer lettered in 1603, one does not exist.
cieloCurConAri: The ram with the golden fleece that Jason and the Argonauts would seek: it came down from the sky to save Phrixus and his sister Helle, but she lost her grip and fell into the strait between Europe and Asia that bears her name, the Hellespont. The spring equinox was called the “first point of Aries”; precession has carried it some 30° on, into Pisces.
cieloCurConAur: The charioteer: most commonly he is taken to be Erichthonius, legendary king of Athens and the first to harness four horses to a chariot. Of the chariot itself, though, there is no sign in the sky, and no legend explains why he is so laden with livestock: he carries a she-goat, Capella, the sixth-brightest star in the sky, which according to Aratus is Amaltheia, the goat that suckled Zeus, and beside her two kids, Eta and Zeta Aurigae. One star he shared with Taurus: the bull kept the tip of its horn and the charioteer lost his right foot.
cieloCurConBoo: The herdsman, already found in the Odyssey. For some he is Arcas, son of Zeus and of Callisto, the Great Bear; for others Icarius, whom Dionysus taught to make wine: the shepherds he shared it with got so drunk that their friends thought they had been poisoned, and killed him. Its Arcturus, “the bear guard”, is the fourth-brightest star in the sky. And his dogs, Canes Venatici, may have been born of a mistranslation from Arabic: “the crook” misread as “the dogs”.
cieloCurConCae: The engraver’s chisel: two crossed tools tied with a ribbon, as Lacaille drew them. “There are no legends associated with the constellation”: its only story is that of its name, from les Burins to Caelum Scalptorium and then plain Caelum, proposed by John Herschel in 1844 and adopted by Francis Baily in 1845. Its stars never get brighter than fourth magnitude.
cieloCurConCam: The giraffe, which in Greek was the “camel leopard”: a camel’s neck and a leopard’s spots. Plancius put it on a celestial globe, and Jacob Bartsch, who printed it on a map in 1624, took it for the camel that carried Rebecca to her wedding: for Ridpath, “an unsatisfactory explanation”. A rarity: its Alpha star is not the brightest; Beta is, at magnitude 4.0.
cieloCurConCnc: The crab that bit Heracles’ foot while he fought the Hydra; he crushed it under his heel and Hera, grateful for the attempt, placed it in the sky. It is the faintest constellation of the zodiac — only six stars are brighter than fifth magnitude — but it holds the Beehive (M44), the hazy-looking patch the Greeks called Phatne, the Manger: Praesepe means both “manger” and “hive”.
cieloCurConCVn: The two greyhounds the Herdsman holds on a leash, Asterion (“starry”) and Chara (“dear”), which Hevelius formed from faint stars beneath the tail of the Great Bear. Its chief star is Cor Caroli, “Charles’s heart”, after King Charles I of England, beheaded in 1649. It also holds the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51), some 25 million light years away, the first in which a spiral was seen: Lord Rosse, 1845.
cieloCurConCMa: The great dog, to the Greeks Laelaps, the dog Zeus gave to Europa, which caught whatever it chased; Cephalus took it to Thebes after a fox that could never be caught and, faced with the paradox, Zeus turned both to stone: the dog he placed in the sky, without the fox. It holds Sirius, the most brilliant star in the entire night sky, 8.6 light years away, with a white dwarf companion circling it every 50 years.
cieloCurConCMi: The smaller of Orion’s two dogs. Another story makes it Maera, the dog of Icarius: Icarius is Boötes, his daughter Erigone is Virgo and Maera this dog. Its Procyon, “before the dog”, is the eighth-brightest star in the sky, 11.5 light years away, and it has a white dwarf companion that circles it every 41 years. Ptolemy counted just two stars in it.
cieloCurConCap: The goat with a fish’s tail, descended from the “goat-fish” of the Sumerians and Babylonians. To the Greeks it was the god Pan, who helped the gods against the Titans and warned them of the monster Typhon’s approach, and Zeus set him in the sky. Back then the Sun was here at the winter solstice; precession has moved it to Sagittarius. It is the smallest constellation of the zodiac, less than a third of Virgo.
cieloCurConCar: The keel — in truth the hull — of Argo Navis, the Argonauts’ ship. It holds Canopus, the second-brightest star in the sky, a creamy-white giant just over 300 light years away, which from Tenerife peeps a few degrees above the southern horizon; it is named after Menelaus’s helmsman, who died in Egypt of a snake bite. Eta Carinae flared up brighter than Canopus in 1843 and then all but vanished.
cieloCurConCas: The vain queen of Ethiopia, who boasted she was lovelier than the Nereids and brought punishment on her daughter Andromeda. Her W circles the pole every night, sometimes seated on her throne, sometimes hanging upside down. In November 1572 Tycho Brahe saw a new star in her: a supernova that shone like Venus, magnitude −4, and stayed visible for over a year.
cieloCurConCen: Chiron, the wise centaur and tutor of heroes, wounded by accident with one of Heracles’ poisoned arrows: being immortal he could not die, so Zeus let him pass his immortality to Prometheus. At his foot is Alpha Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, 4.3 light years away; and Omega Centauri, the largest globular cluster in the sky, which Ptolemy logged as a star and Halley recognised as a cluster in 1678. From Tenerife, Alpha Centauri barely skims the southern horizon, but Omega Centauri climbs to about 14°.
cieloCurConCep: The king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda, told by the oracle of Ammon to chain his daughter to appease the sea monster. His most famous star is not his brightest: Delta Cephei is a supergiant that pulses every 5.4 days, the prototype of the Cepheids, the stars used to estimate distances in space.
cieloCurConCet: The sea monster Poseidon sent to ravage the coast of Cepheus’s kingdom, to which Andromeda was offered as a sacrifice and which Perseus killed by driving his sword into its shoulder; in Latin, “whale”. It is the fourth-largest constellation. Its most celebrated star is Mira, “the wonderful”: a red giant that swells and shrinks and changes brightness, recorded by David Fabricius in 1596. And Menkar, “the nostrils”, actually sits on the beast’s jaw.
cieloCurConCha: The chameleon, from the navigators Keyser and de Houtman. The explorer Willem Lodewyckz had reported that “they flick their tongues at flies which they thus catch and eat”, and on Hondius’s globe of 1600 the chameleon flicks its tongue at the neighbouring Fly. Bayer, who misread the insect, drew a bee and called it Apis. Its stars never exceed fourth magnitude.
cieloCurConCir: The pair of dividers used by geometers, draughtsmen and navigators, which Lacaille squeezed, folded, into an almost non-existent gap between the forefeet of the Centaur and the Southern Triangle. It is the smallest of his 14 inventions and the fourth-smallest constellation in the whole sky. In his text he called it “the geometer’s compasses”.
cieloCurConCol: The dove Noah sent out from the Ark to find dry land, which came back with an olive branch in its beak: the sign that the Flood was ending. Others make it the dove the Argonauts released between the Clashing Rocks, to pass safely. Plancius drew it in 1592 from stars Ptolemy had left outside Canis Major. And in the Chinese sky one of its stars was Shi, the droppings from the celestial toilet that lies in Lepus.
cieloCurConCom: Berenice was real: in 246 BC she married her cousin Ptolemy III, king of Egypt, and vowed her hair to the gods if he came back victorious from the war. He did; she cut off her hair and left it in a temple, and the next day it had vanished. The astronomer Conon came to the rescue: the tresses had gone to join the stars, and the court poet Callimachus put it into verse. It is a cluster of faint stars, Melotte 111, which in the Almagest is just “the lock”.
cieloCurConCrA: To the Greeks it was not a crown but a wreath: a circlet of stars at the feet of the Archer, which perhaps slipped off his head, Ridpath jokes. It has no legends of its own, unless it is the crown Dionysus placed in the sky after bringing his mother back from the Underworld. None of its stars is brighter than fourth magnitude, and one of the 13 Ptolemy counted in it is now Alpha Telescopii. The Chinese saw a hard-shelled turtle here, Bie.
cieloCurConCrB: Ariadne’s golden crown, made by Hephaestus and set with jewels from India. Theseus — whom, in one version, its sparkle guided through the labyrinth — abandoned her on the island of Naxos; Dionysus married her and after the wedding tossed the crown into the sky, where its jewels turned into stars. The brightest, Alphecca, was also called Gemma, “the jewel”. To the Chinese the same arc was a prison for working-class miscreants.
cieloCurConCrv: The crow of Apollo, who sent it to fetch water from a spring; the bird dawdled for several days waiting for some figs to ripen and came back with a water snake, which it blamed for blocking the spring. Apollo saw through the lie and condemned it to a life of thirst: perhaps that is why its call is so rasping. In the sky it pecks at the coils of Hydra, with the Cup beside it. Its Alpha is only fourth magnitude: the brightest is Gamma, Gienah.
cieloCurConCrt: Apollo’s cup from the story of the Crow, though to the Greeks it was a krater, the bowl in which wine was mixed with water. It rides on Hydra’s back, tilted towards the crow but just out of the thirsty bird’s reach. As in Corvus, its Alpha is not the brightest: 4.1 against Delta’s 3.6. To the Chinese its stars were part of Yi, the wings of the Red Bird.
cieloCurConCru: The smallest of the 88. Ptolemy knew its stars, but as the hind legs of the Centaur; precession then carried them so far south that Europe lost sight of them, and 16th-century seafarers rediscovered them and began using the cross to find the south celestial pole. Acrux is the most southerly first-magnitude star in the sky. From Tenerife the top three stars peep up less than 5° above the horizon; Acrux, at the foot, never rises.
cieloCurConCyg: The swan Zeus turned into for one of his conquests; from the egg that followed hatched Helen of Troy. Its tail is Deneb, Arabic for “tail”: a supergiant some 1,400 light years away, the most distant of all first-magnitude stars. At the beak is Albireo, a coloured double star, green and amber, whose name looks Arabic but means nothing. Its shape also earns it the name Northern Cross.
cieloCurConDel: The dolphin that found the sea nymph Amphitrite when she fled from Poseidon and won her over; the grateful god placed it among the stars. Its best story is modern: two of its stars are called Sualocin and Rotanev, which read backwards spell Nicolaus Venator, the Latinised name of Niccolò Cacciatore, Piazzi’s assistant at Palermo; they appeared in the 1814 catalogue. It is usually said that Cacciatore named them himself, which would make him the only person to have named a star after himself and got away with it; but, as Ridpath notes, Piazzi may just as well have named them to honour his heir apparent, his “dauphin”.
cieloCurConDor: Not a pond goldfish but the dolphinfish of the open sea, known elsewhere as mahi-mahi: Dutch navigators saw it chasing flying fish, and in the sky, too, it follows the Flying Fish. It holds most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy some 170,000 light years away, and in it the Tarantula Nebula, so bright that Bayer drew it in 1603 as if it were a star. Kepler called it Xiphias, the swordfish.
cieloCurConDra: Ladon, the dragon that guarded the tree of the golden apples and could speak in different voices. Heracles killed it with his poisoned arrows to steal the apples, and Hera placed it in the sky, where Hercules still has his foot on its head. It is the eighth-largest constellation, yet not very striking: it coils around the pole, its tail between the two bears. Its Alpha, Thuban, is not the brightest; Gamma, Eltanin, is, from the Arabic for “the serpent”.
cieloCurConEqu: The foal, the second-smallest constellation in the sky, of which only the head is seen, next to that of Pegasus. Perhaps Ptolemy (or Hipparchus) had in mind Hippe, daughter of the centaur Chiron, who was seduced by Aeolus; when her father came looking for her, she begged the gods for help and they turned her into a mare. Artemis placed her in the sky, where she still hides from Chiron, the Centaur, showing only her head. Ridpath thinks its true inventor was Hipparchus rather than Ptolemy.
cieloCurConEri: The river into which Phaethon fell, the son of the Sun who insisted on driving his father’s chariot: he lost control and Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt; his hair streaming fire, he plunged into the Eridanus like a shooting star. It is the sixth-largest constellation. For Ptolemy the river ended 17° farther north, at the star we now call Acamar; Achernar, “the river’s end”, was too far south for him, and it is the only first-magnitude star missing from the Almagest.
cieloCurConFor: The chemists’ distillation furnace, which Lacaille tucked into a bend of the river Eridanus. It is sometimes said that he invented it to honour Lavoisier, but that is a misunderstanding: when his chart was published, Lavoisier was 13 years old. The curious thing is that it did end up linked to him: in 1801 Bode redrew it from Lavoisier’s apparatus for splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen and renamed it Apparatus Chemicus, a name that never stuck.
cieloCurConGem: Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Leda: Pollux, son of Zeus, was immortal; Castor, son of a king, was not. When Castor died, run through by a sword, Pollux asked Zeus to share his immortality with him, and they stayed together in the sky, embracing. They were the patrons of sailors, who saw them in the St Elmo’s fire on the masts. Castor is Alpha, yet it is almost half a magnitude fainter than Pollux, and it is not one star but a system of six.
cieloCurConGru: The crane, though it could have been another bird: de Houtman called it “the heron” in his catalogue of 1603, and in 1605 it appeared as the flamingo; the crane won, a bird the Greeks held sacred to Hermes. Its head, the star Gamma, was for Ptolemy the tip of the Southern Fish’s tail, and its Alpha is called Alnair, from the Arabic for “the bright one from the fish’s tail”.
cieloCurConHer: To the Greeks he was just “the kneeling one”: “no one knows his name, nor what he labours at”, wrote Aratus. It was Eratosthenes who identified him as Heracles, with lion’s skin and club, his left foot on the head of the Dragon. Many of his labours are in the sky: the Nemean lion is Leo; the Hydra and the crab that bit him are constellations, and the Dragon is Ladon, guardian of the golden apples. It is the fifth-largest constellation.
cieloCurConHor: The pendulum clock beating the seconds of Lacaille’s observations, of the type Christiaan Huygens invented in 1656, though his was much simpler. In the sky it has a fully marked dial and even a seconds hand. In 1899 R. H. Allen gave it the name Horologium Oscillatorium, but Lacaille never called it that; and Bode drew it with a gridiron pendulum, the kind John Harrison invented in 1726.
cieloCurConHya: The largest of the 88: it winds over a quarter of the way around the sky, 102.5° from end to end. It is the water snake of Lerna, whose breath killed and whose heads grew back, overcome by Heracles in his second labour with the help of his charioteer Iolaus, who burned each stump. In the myth it had nine heads; in the sky it has only one. Its only star of note is Alphard, from the Arabic for “the solitary one”.
cieloCurConHyi: The male water snake, not to be confused with Hydra, which is female and much larger: these are the sea snakes the Dutch navigators would have seen on their voyages. No constellation has been redrawn as often. Bayer had it pass through the south celestial pole; Lacaille docked its tail to make room for his Octant and rerouted it between the two Magellanic Clouds. Its brightest stars are third magnitude, and none has a name.
cieloCurConInd: A native brandishing a spear as though hunting, but nobody knows where he is from: perhaps the East Indies or southern Africa, perhaps Madagascar, where the Dutch fleet stayed for several months, or perhaps he stands for all the peoples the navigators met. His portrait has changed a lot: Bayer showed him face-on, spear in his left hand; in Hevelius’s atlas he looks like a woman, and Bode turned him round, seen from the back, perhaps to make him right-handed.
cieloCurConLac: The lizard, squeezed by Hevelius between the Swan and Andromeda “like a lizard between rocks”. He also called it Stellio, the name of a lizard, the starred agama, a name that fell out of use and that the IAU has revived for its star Alpha. It has no legends; its brightest stars are fourth magnitude, and the Greek letters were given not by Hevelius but by Francis Baily in 1845. To the Chinese its northern part was the centre of Tengshe, the flying serpent, a figure that spread into the neighbouring constellations.
cieloCurConLeo: The Nemean lion, killed by Heracles in the first of his twelve labours: he blocked one of the two entrances to its cave, went in by the other and choked it with his arm. On its chest is Regulus, Latin for “little king”, which to the Babylonians was already “the king”; the name is sometimes said to be Copernicus’s invention, but he was only one of the first to use it. Six stars form the sickle of its head and chest, and the tuft of its tail is now Coma Berenices.
cieloCurConLMi: The lion cub accompanying Leo, which Hevelius formed from eighteen faint stars between the Great Bear and Leo. It has no legends, but it does have an anomaly: when Francis Baily handed out the Greek letters in 1845 he gave Beta to the second star and, by an oversight, forgot the brightest one. So Leo Minor has a Beta but no Alpha; that star, 46 LMi, is now called Praecipua, “the chief one”.
cieloCurConLep: The hare crouching at Orion’s feet, endlessly chased by the Great Dog. Hermes placed it in the sky for its swiftness, but there is another story: on the island of Leros there were no hares until someone brought in a pregnant female; everyone started breeding them, they overran the fields and destroyed the crops, until the islanders drove them out together. Its image was set in the sky as a reminder that you can easily end up with too much of a good thing. The Chinese saw here a well for the army and a toilet.
cieloCurConLib: The only constellation of the zodiac that is not a living being: the scales of justice held up by the goddess next door, Virgo. To the Greeks, and still to Ptolemy, these were the claws of the Scorpion; the balance took hold among the Romans in the 1st century BC. Its two main stars remember it: Zubenelgenubi, “the southern claw”, and Zubeneschamali, “the northern claw”, which shines a little brighter than Alpha.
cieloCurConLup: To the Greeks it was just “the wild beast”, Therion, and to the Romans “the beast”: the animal the Centaur carries impaled on a long pole towards the Altar, as if to sacrifice it. The wolf identity took hold in the Renaissance. It has no Greek myths, probably because it is an imported constellation: to the Babylonians it was UR.IDIM, “the wild dog” or “the wolf”. None of its stars had a name until 2024, when the IAU called the brightest one Uridim, after that old name.
cieloCurConLyn: Hevelius formed it from stars so faint that, as he put it, anyone wishing to see it would need “the eyesight of a lynx”. Whether he also had the mythological Lynceus in mind is not known. Only one of its stars has a Greek letter, Alpha, magnitude 3.1, given by Francis Baily. And it has intruders: two stars Flamsteed catalogued in the Great Bear actually lie in the Lynx, and some charts label a “10 UMa” here.
cieloCurConLyr: The lyre of Orpheus, which Hermes made from a tortoise shell with seven strings, one for each Pleiad. With it Orpheus went down to the underworld for Eurydice, on one condition: not to look back until they were in daylight again. He looked, and lost her for ever. Its Vega is the fifth-brightest star in the sky; the name comes from the Arabic for “the swooping eagle”, and Bode spelled it Wega.
cieloCurConMen: Table Mountain at Cape Town, from where Lacaille catalogued the southern stars in 1751 and 1752. And it has its “table-cloth”: part of the Large Magellanic Cloud caps it like the white cloud that settles on the real mountain with the south-easterly wind. Its brightest stars are only fifth magnitude.
cieloCurConMic: The compound microscope, the kind with more than one lens, which Lacaille put on his 1756 chart using six stray stars Ptolemy had left outside the Southern Fish. Its brightest star, Gamma, is magnitude 4.7. Ridpath sums it up without mercy: “the only remarkable thing about Microscopium is that anyone could imagine a separate constellation here”.
cieloCurConMon: The unicorn, unknown to the Greeks: Plancius put it on a celestial globe; it fills a large area between Hydra and Orion where there was no Greek constellation. Jacob Bartsch pointed in his book to passages of the Bible that supposedly mention unicorns, now regarded as mistranslations. Its brightest stars are fourth magnitude, and Beta outshines Alpha; what is worth seeing is the Rosette Nebula, a wreath-shaped mass of glowing gas with embedded stars.
cieloCurConMus: The fly with the Chameleon beside it: on their stopover on Madagascar, the Dutch navigators had seen chameleons eating flies. Its name has flitted about: de Houtman called it “the fly”; Bayer, “the bee”, and so it was known for two centuries; Plancius, Muia, Greek for “fly”. And for a time it was the Southern Fly, because in the northern sky there was another fly that is no longer among the 88.
cieloCurConNor: The architect’s set-square and ruler, by Lacaille, next to his other surveying and drawing instruments, the Compasses and the Southern Triangle. R. H. Allen misread the French map and called it “the Level and Square”, an error which, as Ridpath says, “has caused confusion ever since”. Its brightest stars are only fourth magnitude and none has a name; when the modern boundaries were fixed, its Alpha and Beta passed to Scorpius.
cieloCurConOct: The octant, the instrument navigators used to measure the height of the pole, invented in 1730 by John Hadley; Lacaille placed it exactly where it is needed: around the south celestial pole. There is no southern Pole Star: the nearest naked-eye star to the pole, Sigma Octantis, is magnitude 5.4, barely visible. And its Alpha, magnitude 5.2, is the faintest of all the Alpha stars in the sky.
cieloCurConOph: The serpent-bearer: Asclepius, the god of medicine, who became able to raise the dead; Hades complained to Zeus, who struck him down with a thunderbolt and then made him immortal in the sky. The Sun crosses it in early December, which is why it is sometimes called “the 13th sign of the zodiac”. Here lies Barnard’s Star, 5.9 light years away, and here in 1604 shone Kepler’s supernova, the last seen in our galaxy.
cieloCurConOri: The hunter who boasted he could kill every animal on Earth; Gaia, enraged, sent a scorpion after him, which is why Orion and Scorpius are never in the sky at the same time. In Egypt he was Sah, a god linked with Osiris. His belt is the Three Marys, as it is called in Spain and most of Latin America; from it hangs the sword, with the Orion Nebula, which even to the naked eye is clearly not a star. And around 20 October each year the Orionids seem to stream out of here: dust from Halley’s Comet.
cieloCurConPav: The peacock, Hera’s sacred bird, whose chariot was drawn by peacocks. When Hermes lulled Argus to sleep, the hundred-eyed watchman guarding Io, Hera set those eyes on the peacock’s tail. But the one in the sky is not the blue peacock of India but its larger, showier and more aggressive cousin, the Java green peacock. Its Alpha is simply called Peacock: the name was given around 1937 by the UK’s Nautical Almanac Office for The Air Almanac, the Royal Air Force’s navigation guide.
cieloCurConPeg: The winged horse that sprang from Medusa’s body when Perseus beheaded her; only its front half is drawn. Bellerophon tamed it, and where its hoof struck Mount Helicon, home of the Muses, the spring Hippocrene, “the horse’s fountain”, gushed out. It is the seventh-largest constellation, famous for its Great Square, which really has only three corners of its own: the fourth is now Andromeda’s Alpha.
cieloCurConPer: The hero who beheaded Medusa and saved Andromeda from the sea monster; he is drawn holding the Gorgon’s head. That head is Algol, “the demon’s head”: a star that every 2.9 days dims from magnitude 2.1 to 3.4, because a companion eclipses it; Montanari noticed it in 1671 and John Goodricke timed it in 1783. It also holds the Double Cluster, NGC 869 and NGC 884.
cieloCurConPhe: The phoenix: according to Ovid it lived 500 years, and from the father’s body a new phoenix was born. It is the largest of the twelve constellations drawn by the Dutch navigators at the end of the 16th century. Its brightest star, Ankaa, magnitude 2.4, had earlier been part of a Chinese net for catching birds: a poor spot for a phoenix.
cieloCurConPic: The painter’s easel, with its palette, which Lacaille set beneath the keel of Argo Navis, next to bright Canopus. Its four main stars had already been recorded by de Houtman some 150 years earlier as part of the ship. The name kept shrinking: Equuleus Pictorius in 1763 and, since John Herschel in 1844, plain Pictor.
cieloCurConPsc: Two fish tied by the tails with a cord: Aphrodite and Eros, who fled the monster Typhon by leaping into the Euphrates, where two fish carried them to safety (or they turned into fish themselves); that, it was said, is why the Syrians would not eat fish. It is a disappointingly faint constellation, but an important one: the spring equinox lies here today, and precession will carry it into Aquarius around the year 2597.
cieloCurConPsA: The fish drinking the water that pours from Aquarius’s jar, “a strange thing for a fish to do”, as Ridpath says. Its story comes from Babylon: the Syrian goddess Derceto fell into a lake and was saved by a large fish; that, according to Hyginus, is why the Syrians did not eat fish and worshipped images of fish as gods. Its Fomalhaut, “the fish’s mouth”, is first magnitude, and the Bedouin saw it and Achernar as a pair of ostriches. It was the last constellation in Ptolemy’s catalogue.
cieloCurConPup: The stern of Argo Navis, the Argonauts’ ship, which Lacaille split into three; the rudder separates it from the Keel, and Canopus, which sits on the rudder, stayed with the Keel. Because Lacaille shared out the Greek letters over the whole ship, the Stern has neither Alpha nor Beta: its brightest star is Zeta, Naos, Greek for “ship”. And in Bode’s atlas of 1801, half hidden behind the hind quarters of the Great Dog, lurks a scaly sea creature whose identity is unknown.
cieloCurConPyx: The seaman’s compass, which Lacaille set beside Argo Navis although it was never part of the ship: the Greeks, in fact, knew nothing of the magnetic compass. For Ptolemy its stars were part of Argo’s mast, and in 1844 John Herschel proposed giving them back to the ship as Malus, “the mast”; that was used for a while, until Gould went back to the compass in 1879. When he Latinised it, Lacaille spelled it with a slip: Pixis Nautica.
cieloCurConRet: The reticle in the eyepiece of the small telescope with which Lacaille measured the southern stars in 1751 and 1752: a diamond-shaped aperture cut out of a copper plate. It lies next to his clock, Horologium, which he used to time each star’s passage through the reticle. As early as 1621 Isaac Habrecht had drawn a rhombus around here; and in 1822 Jamieson tried to replace it with a sundial, Solarium, which only the American Elijah Burritt copied, in his atlas of 1835.
cieloCurConSge: An arrow without a bow, as Aratus already noted, with three possible owners: the one Apollo used to kill the Cyclopes, the one Heracles shot at the eagle that devoured Prometheus’s liver, or Eros’s arrow, which kindled Zeus’s passion for Ganymede. It is the third-smallest constellation in the sky. Its brightest star is Gamma, magnitude 3.5; Alpha, Sham, “the arrow”, only manages 4.4.
cieloCurConSgr: The archer, which the Sumerians already pictured as a winged centaur, PA.BIL.SAG; the Greeks took away its wings. Eratosthenes said it was not a centaur, since centaurs did not use bows, but Crotus, son of Eupheme, the Muses’ nurse, and inventor of archery, whom Zeus placed in the sky at their request; Hyginus added that his father was Pan. Today its stars form a teapot, and among them lies the centre of our galaxy, Sagittarius A*. Its Alpha is only the 15th-brightest star in the constellation.
cieloCurConSco: The scorpion that killed Orion, sent by Artemis or by the Earth: the two were placed on opposite sides of the sky, so that Orion sets as the scorpion rises. The Sumerians already called it GIR-TAB, “the scorpion”, over 5,000 years ago. Its claws were its own until, in the 1st century BC, the Romans turned them into Libra. Antares, “like Mars” for its colour, is a supergiant several hundred times the diameter of the Sun; to the Chinese it was “the fire star”, the heart of the Blue Dragon.
cieloCurConScl: The sculptor’s studio, with its table, its tools and a block of marble, as Lacaille drew it; the name kept shrinking until it became plain Sculptor, as John Herschel proposed in 1844. It is the largest of Lacaille’s 14 inventions, although its stars are fourth magnitude and fainter and none of them has a name. In 1801 Bode took away the marble and in its place created another constellation, Machina Electrica, an electrical machine that did not survive.
cieloCurConSct: The shield of King John III Sobieski of Poland, which Hevelius placed in the sky in 1684 out of gratitude: the king had helped him rebuild his observatory after the fire of 1679. It is the only constellation introduced for political reasons that is still in use, though it nearly vanished: Flamsteed and Baily left it out. Halley had dedicated another to his king, Charles II of England, Robur Carolinum, and that one did not survive. Its gem is the Wild Duck Cluster, shaped like a flight of ducks.
cieloCurConSer: The only constellation split in two: the head and tail of the serpent, on either side of Ophiuchus, who holds it. Ophiuchus is Asclepius; why he wrestles with a serpent is not fully explained, but his link with snakes comes from a story: Asclepius once killed a snake and saw another bring it back to life by placing a herb on it; he used the same trick on the dead. Snakes, which shed their skins every year, were a symbol of rebirth. Its most celebrated object is M16, a star cluster inside the Eagle Nebula, the one with the gas “pillars” photographed by Hubble.
cieloCurConSex: The sextant with which Hevelius measured star positions, destroyed with his other instruments when his house burned in 1679. Hevelius made naked-eye sightings with his sextant all his life, though he used telescopes for the Moon and planets; perhaps he formed this constellation from such faint stars to show off the keenness of his eyes: the brightest is magnitude 4.5 and none has a name. To the Chinese, three of them were Tianxiang, the celestial minister.
cieloCurConTau: Zeus turned into the handsomest bull in the herd to carry off Europa: she ventured to sit on his back and he swam away with her to Crete. Only the front half of the bull is drawn. Its reddish eye, Aldebaran, looks like one of the Hyades but lies in front of them, 65 light years away, less than half the distance of the cluster, which lies at 150; the Romans called the Hyades “the piglets”. The Pleiades ride on its back.
cieloCurConTel: One of those immensely long aerial telescopes hung from a mast, like the ones Cassini used at the Paris Observatory: they were made that long to reduce the false colour produced by the crude lenses of the time. Lacaille drew it so tall that it reached up between Sagittarius and Scorpius, and later it was cut back: its old Beta is now Eta Sagittarii, and its Theta the humble 45 Ophiuchi. Its brightest star, Alpha, is magnitude 3.5.
cieloCurConTri: To the Greeks it was the Deltoton, for its shape like a capital delta, Δ: Eratosthenes saw in it the Nile delta, and others Sicily, the Trinacria of the ancients, home of the goddess Ceres. Here lies M33, the Triangulum Galaxy, in our Local Group, visible with binoculars. In 1687 Hevelius added a smaller triangle next to it and called this one the Greater Triangle; the small one no longer exists. Its brightest star, Beta, had no official name until November 2025, when the IAU gave it an Arabic one: Alaybasan.
cieloCurConTrA: Brighter than its northern sibling: its three main stars outshine those of Triangulum. Lacaille drew it with a plumb bob hanging from it, like a surveyor’s level, and R. H. Allen, by mistake, transferred the name “level” to neighbouring Norma, confusing generations of astronomers. Its Alpha is called Atria, a contraction coined by navigators from its scientific name, Alpha Trianguli Australis.
cieloCurConTuc: The toucan, a South American bird, which suggests it might have been invented by Keyser, who had been there before the voyage to the East Indies; de Houtman, by contrast, was describing an oriental hornbill. Behind its tail lies the Small Magellanic Cloud, and beside it 47 Tucanae, rated the second-best globular cluster in the sky. That 47 comes from Bode: Lacaille gave it no number.
cieloCurConUMa: Callisto, the companion of Artemis whom Zeus took by force and who ended up as a bear: for 15 years she roamed the woods in a bear’s body with a human mind. Zeus raised her to the sky and made her son Arcas into Boötes. Hera persuaded Tethys and Oceanus never to let her bathe in the northern waters: that is why, from mid-northern latitudes, the bear never sets; from Tenerife, farther south, part of it does dip below the horizon. And that long tail real bears lack? In a joke by Thomas Hood, the tails got stretched when Zeus pulled the bears up into the sky.
cieloCurConUMi: The bear the Phoenicians steered by, rather than the Great Bear; the Greeks said it was measured out by the sage Thales of Miletus. Aratus called it Kynosoura, “the dog’s tail”, the origin of the English word cynosure, “guiding star”. At the tip of its tail is Polaris, less than 1° from the north celestial pole, which it will approach most closely around the year 2100; in Ptolemy’s day there was no bright star near the pole. And its star Yildun owes its name to a misspelling of the Turkish word for “star”.
cieloCurConVel: The sails of Argo Navis, the Argonauts’ ship, which Lacaille split into three; since he had given the letters Alpha and Beta to the two brightest stars of Carina, the Sails were left with neither, and for fainter stars Lacaille had to turn to Roman letters. Two of its stars, with two of Carina, form the False Cross, sometimes mistaken for the Southern Cross although it is larger and fainter. Its brightest star, Gamma Velorum, is a double of combined magnitude 1.7.
cieloCurConVir: Dike, goddess of justice, who lived among humans in the Golden Age; when they turned wicked she withdrew to the mountains and finally flew up to the sky, where she still sits beside Libra, which some see as the scales of justice. It is the second-largest constellation, behind only Hydra. In her hand shines Spica, “the ear of grain”, and Vindemiatrix is “the grape-gatherer”. The autumn equinox lies here: it crossed from Libra into Virgo around 730 BC.
cieloCurConVol: The flying fish, which sometimes landed on ships’ decks and was used for food. In the sky the Dorado chases it, just as at sea. It was called Piscis Volans until John Herschel proposed in 1844 shortening it to plain Volans. Its brightest stars are only fourth magnitude, and it has no legends.
cieloCurConVul: The fox with the goose, as Hevelius called it, explaining that the fox was taking the goose to Cerberus for a shared breakfast. Since then the goose has flown, or been eaten, leaving just the fox; but in 2017 the IAU gave the name back to the star Alpha, on the fox’s nose, which is now called Anser, “goose”. On its border with Sagitta lies an asterism shaped like a clothes hanger, the Coathanger.
